He did not know that his true son had been left safely behind, grown strong, and was fated soon to beat him in battle and to drive him out of kingdom and honor, to be king among the undying: in the beautiful Cretan cave and its dark nest of Gaia's care, where the baby fed and slept and cried alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 480-492 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Zeus was full-grown, in limbs and thought, he made Cronos vomit up his children out of Gaia's counsels and will fight and unchanging strength; and he had swallowed the stone last of all, so it came up again first, and Zeus set it down in the earth at Pytho under Parnassus, to stand there forever a wonder to mortal men. Then he freed his uncles the Cyclopes from Cronos's cruel bonds, and they gave him thunder and glowing thunderbolt and lightning, which earth had once hidden; and it was by these that Zeus rules both mortals and immortals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 492-506 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

region.zh: 墨科涅（近希吉昂，神話地理）

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Michael Heumann (2021), lines ca. 535-616

texts.license: Poem public domain; translation CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Heumann 2021) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: When gods and mortals met for a shared feast at Mecone, Prometheus divided an ox between the two sides, hiding the meat under the stomach-skin and the bare bones under glistening fat, and let Zeus choose. Zeus chose plausibly in anger, discovered the deception, and has raged ever since; the trick settles forever the rule that men may eat the flesh while the smoke-borne bones are the gods' due, and leads — through fire and Pandora — to the condition of mortal life.
summary.zh: 神與人於墨科涅共宴之際，普羅米修斯將牛分為兩堆：肉藏於胃皮之下，白骨覆以油亮脂肪，請宙斯自選。宙斯自以識破而選白骨，卻中了圈套、勃然大怒。這場戲就此定下祭祀規矩——人食其肉、敬神得骨——並因盜火與潘多拉之事引出人類勞苦的命運。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When the gods and mortal men came to order a feast together at Mecone, Prometheus, glorious son of Iapetus, cut up a great ox and divided it with cunning. He set before Zeus the flesh and the rich entrails, wrapping them handsomely in the ox's belly, and then heaped up the bones of the white ox and hid them under a mantle of shining fat, so the eye saw the prizes at a glance and the abundance of the meal lay on the lesser part.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 535-545 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: Said Zeus, father of gods and men, to him in mock-affection: son of Iapetus, most brilliant of gods, good friend, you have divided these portions quite unfairly. And Prometheus answered with a smile: great Zeus, pick whichever of the two hands your heart desires. He said it meaning to trick him; but Zeus, already seeing through it, took the white fat in both hands, and in anger, sorrow, and rage, when his heart burned when he saw the bones underneath it and grasped how he had been cheated, planned against mortal men a terrible sorrow to come in payment for the fire to be stolen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 545-560 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Zeus spoke aloud his judgment, warningly: so, son of Iapetus, most brilliant of all, you have not lost your skill at dividing. And by his word, ever since then, the tribes of men upon the earth burned white bones of oxen upon smoking altars for the deathless ones — the ritual rule set in that trick over the kill: the gods partake of scent and smoke, and men eat the substance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 556-560 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: In retaliation, Zeus withheld fire from the fire-trees of the earth so that mortals could not boil nor forge; but Prometheus stole the far-shining flame again in a hollow fennel stalk. Rage shook Zeus then: in reprisal for the stolen gift of fire he had Hephaestus mould a maiden out of earth and water, dressed her beautifully and crowned her, and had her sent down among men as a gift the likes of which Epimetheus took to his sorrow — the price of fire, Pandora, the mould-born evil who founded the whole race of womankind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 560-616 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ten-Year War of the Titans

region.zh: 奧特里斯山與奧林波斯山（神話地理）

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Michael Heumann (2021), lines ca. 617-735

texts.license: Poem public domain; translation CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Heumann 2021) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: For ten years the young gods from Olympus and the Titans on Othrys grind one another without result. Zeus frees the Hundred-Handed from their long prison in the deep, feeds them nectar and ambrosia, and turns the balance; three hundred stones thrown by three giants smash the Titans' hosts. Zeus hurls them down beneath the earth to Tartarus, guarded by his new allies.
summary.zh: 奧林波斯的新神與奧特里斯山的提坦纏鬥十年不分勝負。宙斯釋放長年囚於黑暗的百手三巨人，以仙食仙飲壯其氣力，戰局立轉；三百塊巨石接連砸下，提坦大軍潰敗，被宙斯投向大地深處的塔耳塔羅斯，由百手巨人看守。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Ouranos had long ago bound the Hundred-Handed — Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges — in strong chains for their reckless, terrifying size and hid them beneath the broad earth. But the sons of Cronos brought them up to the light at Gaia's own telling, having learned that with them the victory would be theirs against the Titans: the three sat sullenly below the earth's rim, suffering enormous grief, until the son of Cronos and the immortal gods set them free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 617-635 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the two sides staked their strengths at war: the Titan gods on high Othrys, the younger gods gathered on Olympus, who were born to fair-haired Rhea after bed with Cronos; and for ten long years without end they fought one another, hearts and anger taut with fury, and the battle gave no decision to either side, since the victory was shared equally between the blowing thorns of the two proud families.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 635-655 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Zeus gave the Hundred-Handed nectar and ambrosia to eat and drink, the food of the undying, and their souls grew high; and the master of gods spoke to them: you, brightnesses from below, remember my kindness in freeing you from the stony prison and the grievous darkness; now with your untouchable hands stand against the Titans in their battles for us. And Cottus answered for them all: they knew his famous mind; with clear minds and quivering strength they would battle for his kingship in the fearsome war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 655-685 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: They armed that day and drew lines of battle, and with them Zeus from heaven hurled bolt after bolt, the crash of the sky, wrapped in a twisting flame; the life-bearing earth boomed and burned; the rivers, the streams of Oceanus, and the endless sea boiled, and the hot blast carried to the Aether of both sides; and blind-eyed Chaos reeled and shuddered. Then the Hundred-Handed rose from among the front lines and hurled hails of stones, three hundred boulders one after another; the Titans buried the sky no more, and were thrown under the whole earth and bound there; the drop to murky Tartarus is more than nine days' fall for a bronze anvil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 685-730 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

title.en: Zeus and Typhon, the Last Challenger

region.zh: 阿里馬亞，大地深處（神話地理）

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Michael Heumann (2021), lines ca. 820-880

texts.license: Poem public domain; translation CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Heumann 2021) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: Gaia's comeback after the defeat of the Titans is a last child begotten on Tartarus itself: Typhon, whose shoulders sprout a hundred snake-heads with flickering tongues of fire, whose hundred voices bellow, roar, yelp and hiss. One day's contest would have ended with Typhon king over gods and men, had Zeus not watched: he leaps from Olympus and burns the heads away, hurls the monster lame into Tartarus, and settles forever the weather-winds that still wreck ships and harvests.
summary.zh: 提坦敗亡後，該亞的最後反撲是與塔耳塔羅斯所生的堤豐：肩上百顆蛇頭、吐信帶火，百聲齊鳴，可獅吼、牛吼、犬吠、蛇嘶。若非宙斯戒備，一日之戰堤豐便將稱王。宙斯自奧林波斯躍下，燒盡百顆頭顱，擊癱巨怪擲入塔耳塔羅斯；他化為的風暴狂風，至今仍是損毀船隻與莊稼的天災。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: When Zeus had driven the Titans out of heaven, huge Gaia bore with Tartarus her youngest child, Typhon, whose hands were made for deeds of strength and whose feet were tireless. On his shoulders sat a hundred snake-heads of a fearsome dragon, each in its own pattern; his eyes flashed fire from every head, every head glared flame on every side, and fire darted from every one of all those glares and mouths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 820-835 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: Every voice in all the heads poured out voices unspeakable: sometimes such as the gods might understand, sometimes the bellow of a furious bull, sometimes like the proud roar of a lion, sometimes like whelps beneath their mother, wondrous to hear, sometimes hissing tall mountain-music, so that a terrible echo went round the rocks. Had not the father of gods and men been watching, that day would have ended with Typhon king over mortals and immortals alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 830-845 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zeus thundered hard and mightily, and the earth about him, the sky above him, the sea, the courses of Ocean, and Tartarus itself shook. Great Olympus trembled under the immortal feet of the king as he came leaping in with his weapons, and all around him heat and flame and thunder exploded; the violet sea was consumed by the heat of the fire and flame and hasty wind and blazing lightnings, and the undying earth and sea and sky boiled over. The crash and the quaking came down deep into Tartarus, and Cronos and the Titans who lived there trembled with fear under the endless roar of the terrible combat-strife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 845-860 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

passages.text: With thunder and lightning in his grip Zeus leapt out and burnt all the marvelous heads about the tremendous monster; and when he had beaten him down with blows, that huge thing fell lame, and the broad earth groaned. Flames went out from the thunder-lord into the cliff-girt dells below, burning much of the strange earth, melting it like tin in a skillful youth's crucible, or iron tamed in mountain dells by blazing fire: so the earth melted in the flash of the thunderbolt. With wrath in his heart Zeus threw him whole into wide Tartarus; and out of Typhon the strength of the wet, blowing winds is always blowing, useless winds whose storms toss ships and drown sailors and wreck the works of men upon the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 860-880 (Heumann 2021); not verbatim.

region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Christopher Kelk (2020), lines ca. 106-210

texts.license: Poem public domain; translation © 2020 Chris Kelk (free non-commercial use) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: A second story for Perses, 'which I will tell you skilfully': the gods made first a golden race under Cronus, then silver, then bronze, then a noble race of heroes swallowed up by war at Thebes and Troy, and finally the iron race — Hesiod's own — in which he wishes he had not been born.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德再講一則故事給佩耳塞斯：諸神先在克洛諾斯治下造黃金一族，其後白銀、青銅，再造亡於忒拜與特洛伊戰爭的英雄族，最後是鐵之族——詩人所在的當世，勞苦無休、父子相疏、義理蕩然，他寧願自己未生於此世。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The gods who dwell on Olympus first made a golden race of men who lived in the time of Cronus, when he ruled in heaven. They lived like gods with care-free hearts, remote from toil and misery; and dismal age did not abide with them, but they danced away from pain; and they rejoiced in festivals, with the dear gods nearby. Then in death they lay as if overcome by sleep; and all good things were theirs, for the fruitful earth unasked would bring forth for them fruits in their season, so that freely, in peace and quiet, they drove back the land with many flocks. This race was buried beneath the earth, but they became, by high Zeus's device, holy spirits upon the earth, guardians of mortal men — watching over judgments and wicked deeds, girded in mist, roaming everywhere over the earth, givers of wealth: this kingly office was theirs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 106-135 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they who dwell on Olympus made a second race, of silver, far inferior, in body and in mind. A child was bred up a hundred years at his mother's knee, playing about the house, a great bawling innocent; but when they grew up and came to their full measure, they lived but a brief time in suffering and sorrow, through their own foolishness; they could not hold back their own arrogance, and they were not willing to worship the blessed gods, nor to sacrifice upon the holy altars of the blessed ones, as is due law among men. Then Zeus, in wrath, hid them under the earth, because they gave no honour to the blessed gods who dwell on Olympus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 140-155 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zeus the father made a third race, of bronze, in no wise like the ones of old: terrible and strong men, all their delight in works of war and violence; their food was not the grain of the earth, and their limbs and souls were of adamant; their weapons were bronze, their houses bronze, their tools of bronze, for as yet there was no black iron. They were brought down by their own hands, and went down nameless to the mouldy house of chill Hades, never seen again once black death had taken them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 155-170 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, upon the earth, Zeus son of Cronus made a fourth race, more just and better: the godly race of heroes, who are called half-gods, the race before ours on the boundless earth. But evil war and the dread battle-line destroyed some of them — some at seven-gated Thebes, in Cadmus' land, dying for the flocks of Oedipus; and others brought in ships over the great gulf of the sea to Troy for the sake of fair-haired Helen. There some were covered by the earth; but to others Zeus the father, son of Cronus, gave life and homes apart from men, at the ends of the earth, where they dwell with carefree hearts in the Isles of the Blessed by the deep-eddying ocean; and the earth bears them sweet fruit three times a year, while Cronus still rules among them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 170-190 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Zeus made a fifth race, of men upon the bountiful earth, and I wish, he said, that I may not be among them; but either I had died before, or been born afterwards. For now the race is indeed one of iron; and never by day shall they rest from toil and sorrow, nor by night from being worn away; and the gods shall give them heavy troubles. Yet even so good shall be mingled with their evils. And Zeus shall destroy this race too, when children are born with grey hair on their temples. Nor shall the father be one with his children, nor children with their father, nor guest with host, nor comrade with comrade, nor shall brother be dear to brother as of old. Men shall dishonour their parents as soon as they are old, reviling them with hard words; and there shall be no grace for the man who keeps his oath, nor for the just, nor for the good: the devouring of wrong shall prosper, and shame shall no longer be. And at the last, from the broad-pathed earth, Majesty and Awe, wrapped in fair robes, shall leave the dwelling of men and go up to Olympus, forsaking mankind; and there shall be nothing left against the evil but sorrow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 190-210 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Christopher Kelk (2020), lines ca. 202-285

texts.license: Poem public domain; translation © 2020 Chris Kelk (free non-commercial use) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: To his brother Perses, who has taken him to law before bribed judges, Hesiod tells a fable: a hawk gripping a nightingale in its talons mocks the small bird's crying — the strong can do what they like with the weak. But humans are not birds: for them Zeus has established Justice, which blesses the just city and ruins the extortionate.
summary.zh: 對已分產涉訟、賄賂法官的弟弟佩耳塞斯，赫西俄德講了一則寓言：高空中鷹爪抓住夜鶯，嘲弄其可憐哀鳴——強者可任意處置弱者。但人非鳥類：宙斯已為人類立下正義，公正之城因而興盛，貪暴之徒必遭現世報。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod told the lords and judges a fable that they, being wise, could read. A hawk had seized a speckled nightingale in its talons and was carrying it up through the clouds; the little bird hung there weeping out its piteous cry, pierced by the bent claws that held it fast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 202-215 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hawk said to it scornfully: 'Wretched thing, why do you cry out? One far stronger than you holds you; you go wherever I take you. I will make you my dinner if I wish, or I may let you go. He is a fool who tries to contend against those stronger than himself: he loses the struggle and is insulted on top of it.' So spoke the swift-winged bird, the lordly one filled with pride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 215-231 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Perses should listen to justice, and not exalt violence; this is the law the son of Cronus has made for men, for fish and beasts and winged birds eat one another, since there is no justice among them; but to men Zeus has given Justice, which is far the best. A man who knows and declares it, Zeus enriches; but a perjurer who deliberately does wrong has a descendant left to darkness, while his enemy's household prospers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 274-300 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Zeus sent thirty thousand watchers upon the earth, servants of the god, who oversee mankind, mixing unseen, over all the earth; and Justice, the daughter of Zeus, reports to him all crooked judgments. When judges swallow bribes, woe to the city: plague and famine come, women are barren, and houses dwindle. But when straight judgments are given, the city blooms, children grow, the earth yields acorns and honey, the sheep are heavy with wool, and there is abundance on the earth. So Hesiod warned the gift-swallowing lords to straighten the crooked decisions, for the watcher sees all, and the eye of Zeus observes all things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 240-285 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（赫西俄德故鄉，象徵性定位）

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Christopher Kelk (2020), lines ca. 57-105

texts.license: Poem public domain; translation © 2020 Chris Kelk (free non-commercial use) — paraphrase only in this record

summary.en: Because Prometheus stole fire, Zeus commissions a trap for men: Hephaestus fashions a maiden from clay, each god contributes an ornament or a flaw — beauty, weaving, lies, a shameless nature — and she is called Pandora. Hermes delivers her to Epimetheus, who forgets his brother's warning; she opens the great jar and scatters the whole race of ills upon mankind, keeping only Hope inside under the lid.
summary.zh: 因普羅米修斯盜火，宙斯設計陷害人類：赫菲斯托斯以黏土塑造少女，諸神各贈其一飾或一病——美貌、織布、謊言與羞怯——並名之潘多拉。赫爾墨斯將她送至厄庇墨透斯，他忘卻兄長的警告；她揭開大罐，人間從此疾病苦難橫行，唯希望獨存於罐中。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; the myth carries Hesiod's misogyny and is presented as historical material without endorsement.

passages.text: In spite over the theft, Zeus prepared a second mischief to afflict mankind. He ordered the celebrated lame god, famed Hephaestus, to mix earth and water and to put in it the voice and strength of a human being, with the face of a goddess, a beautiful, sweet-looking girl. Athena was to teach her woman's skills, to weave richly-worked cloth of various kinds; golden Aphrodite was to pour grace about her head and painful desire and heavy-weariness that shakes the limbs; Hermes, the Argus-killer, was to add a dog's mind and a thieving disposition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 57-90 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Zeus's word the famed lame god immediately moulded the likeness of a modest maiden from the earth, as Cronus's son had commanded. The grey-eyed queen Athena arrayed her and fastened her girdle; the divine Graces and our lady Persuasion hung golden necklaces upon her; the fair-tressed Hours crowned her with spring flowers; and Pallas Athena adorned her person fully. And in her breast the Argus-killer Hermes, by the contriving of loud-thundering Zeus, put lies and guile, a thieving nature, and a shameless spirit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 90-100 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: Since all the Olympians had given a gift, her name was called Pandora, Bane of Men, on whose account the gods above all hatched this perfect snare in man's way, sending to Epimetheus the swift messenger of the gods, the Argus-slayer, with the gift. Epimetheus took no thought of the warning that Prometheus had given him — never to receive a gift from Zeus, but to send it back, lest some evil happen to men. He accepted her, and only when he had the evil did he see it at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 90-105 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.

passages.text: For before that no trouble, no disease, and no suffering had ever darkened this race's days: men used to live free of them. But the woman took off the great lid of the jar with her hands and scattered its contents; she dealt portentous griefs to men, and only Hope remained within the unbreakable jar beneath its rim, and did not fly out, because the lid stayed on it, by the will of Aegis-bearing Zeus. But other innumerable troubles wandered among men; the earth was full of evils, and the sea was full. So mankind had diseases to endure day and night of their own accord, in silence, since Zeus devised voicelessness for them. There is no way to escape the will of Zeus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 100-105 (Kelk 2020); not verbatim.
